name: Ptosis surgery (levator advancement)

card.summary: Surgery to raise a drooping upper lid, mainly a functional operation whose appearance benefit (a more open eye) is discussed on forums; supported in medical series.
card.note: Not purely cosmetic in origin; revision surgery and lid asymmetry are possible.

quick.overview:
Ptosis surgery lifts an upper eyelid that sits too low. Levator advancement tightens or reattaches the levator aponeurosis, the tendon that lifts the lid, and is a standard approach for aponeurotic (age- or stretch-related) ptosis.

Beyond vision, looksmaxxing users discuss it for a more open, alert-looking eye. One looksmax.org member shared a before-and-after account of a bilateral repair.
quick.mechanism: Surgeons choose among levator advancement or resection, Muller muscle-conjunctival resection and frontalis sling depending on cause and levator function.
quick.risks: Wikipedia lists uneven lids, dry eye, bleeding, infection and rarely loss of lid movement; one study cited there found about half of surgical patients needed more surgery within 8 to 10 years.

lead: Ptosis surgery lifts an upper eyelid that sits too low (blepharoptosis). For looks, the effect is a wider, more open eye: the lid margin rises off the pupil, the face looks less tired, and the raised brow and forehead wrinkling that people use to compensate can relax.[1][12] Levator advancement, also called aponeurotic ptosis surgery, reattaches or tightens the levator aponeurosis, the tendon that lifts the lid, and is a standard operation for the most common acquired form, which comes from stretching or detachment of that tendon with age, contact-lens wear, eye surgery or rubbing.[2][12][11]

Ptosis can be minimal (1-2 mm), moderate (3-4 mm) or severe (over 4 mm), may affect one or both eyes, and may be congenital or acquired from myogenic, neurogenic, aponeurotic, mechanical or traumatic causes.[1] Patients describe a tired appearance, blurred vision and tearing, and some tilt the head back or lift the lid with a finger.[1] Other operations include Muller muscle-conjunctival resection for mild ptosis with good levator function, levator resection, and frontalis sling procedures using fascia lata or other material for severe cases.[3][4][5][12][17]

The research base consists of anatomy studies, case series and algorithms, surveys, comparative trials of techniques and functional-outcome studies, including one that linked vision-related impairment from ptosis to the impact of surgery.[6][7][10][20][23] Plastic-surgery reviews note that ptosis and eyelid-crease asymmetry can cause significant cosmetic deformity and that precise knowledge of the eyelid anatomy allows precise correction.[19]

On looksmaxxing forums, ptosis repair appears as a way to open the eye and fix lid asymmetry, with first-person accounts of the operation under local anaesthetic and discussion of marginal reflex distance.[13]

paras: A drooping upper lid reduces the height of the eye opening, can cover part of the pupil, and often leads to compensatory frontalis activity, which raises the eyebrows and wrinkles the forehead.[12] An upper lid that has dropped can also leave the lid crease high, faint or missing, and one-sided ptosis makes the eyes look unequal.[12][19] After repair the lid margin sits higher relative to the pupil and the light reflex, and a bilateral repair aims to leave the two lids level.[1][13]

In forum language, ptosis is discussed in terms of eye opening, an alert look and eye-area symmetry. A member of looksmax.org who posted before-and-after images described lids that no longer covered the corneal light reflex the day after surgery, and a replying member called the result a big improvement.[13]

Classification covers myogenic, neurogenic, aponeurotic, mechanical and traumatic causes, and ptosis is usually isolated but can accompany systemic disorders.[1] Marginal reflex distance (MRD) is used to measure severity; Grokipedia gives a normal MRD1 of 4-5 mm.[11] Anatomical studies of the levator palpebrae superioris and orbital septum inform surgical planning.[6][7]

A Nepalese hospital study of 326 ptosis patients over two years described how the type of ptosis varies with age at presentation, with congenital cases presenting younger than acquired ones.[27] An encyclopedia account gives typical ages of presentation of around 68 for aponeurotic ptosis, around 9-12 for congenital ptosis, and the 30s-40s for neurogenic and traumatic ptosis.[12] Ptosis can also accompany conditions such as myasthenia gravis, and reviews of ocular myasthenia describe lid crutches and ptosis surgery among the options once the disease is managed; drugs such as high-dose opioids and occasionally pregabalin, and toxins including botulinum toxin, can cause ptosis as well.[12][26]

Assessment includes history, slit-lamp examination, pupil and eye-movement checks, visual fields, marginal reflex distance and measurement of levator function; surgeons choose between techniques according to these findings.[12][18] A review of blepharoptosis in Seminars in Ophthalmology calls ptosis surgery perhaps the most challenging in oculoplastics, especially in congenital and neuromuscular cases, and says the picture ranges from cosmetic discomfort to severe visual dysfunction.[18]

Aponeurotic surgery was presented as a revival of approaches that preserve tear-producing structures, Muller's muscle and Whitnall's ligament.[2] Muller's muscle-conjunctival resection, with the phenylephrine test used to guide the amount resected, treats minimal to mild ptosis with good levator function,[3][4] and fascia lata harvesting has documented donor-site complications.[5] Paediatric ptosis has been reviewed over 10 years.[9]

A review in Current Opinion in Otolaryngology describes three classic methods: frontalis slings for the most severe cases (with newer materials such as polyester mesh studied as alternatives), conjunctiva-Muller muscle resection with a newer algorithm, and external levator advancement, whose effectiveness was reinforced in a study of congenital ptosis.[17] A 2018 randomised clinical trial compared external levator advancement with Muller muscle-conjunctival resection for aponeurotic blepharoptosis.[20]

The levator operation is commonly done under local anaesthesia with sedation, and a forum member who had it reported a half-hour procedure, brief injection pain and marked swelling the next day.[13] Studies of techniques around the operation include a trial of triamcinolone injection to suppress inflammation after bilateral transcutaneous levator advancement in 32 patients, a trial of tranexamic acid for bleeding in eyelid surgery, and a registered trial of subconjunctival local anaesthetic in anterior ptosis repair.[21][22][29] A 1981 paper described an aponeurotic approach to eyelid retraction, the opposite problem.[25]

Wikipedia lists uneven eyelids, dry eyes, bleeding, infection and rare loss of eyelid movement as risks, and cites a study in which about half of surgical patients needed further surgery within 8 to 10 years.[12]

A national survey by the British Oculoplastic Surgery Society collected practice and outcome data on ptosis surgery in the UK.[23] A study of upper-eyelid surgery measured its effect on corneal topography, one way surgery can alter vision-related measurements.[24] Fascia lata harvesting for sling surgery has its own donor-site effects: in a questionnaire study of 24 patients, early pain on walking (67%), limping (38%) and wound pain (57%) mostly settled within a week, and scar appearance caused minor concern in 38%.[5]
Wikipedia notes ptosis crutch glasses, scleral contact lenses and, since 2020, FDA-approved 0.1% oxymetazoline ophthalmic solution for acquired blepharoptosis.[12]

Wikipedia's oxymetazoline article states that the FDA approved 0.1% oxymetazoline ophthalmic solution (brand Upneeq) for acquired blepharoptosis in July 2020, and that the drug is thought to stimulate adrenergic receptors in Muller's muscle to raise the lid.[30] A Grokipedia page (AI-generated) adds that approval followed in Japan in December 2025 and that it is positioned as an option when surgery is not advisable.[11]

A looksmax.org member posted a personal account of ptosis surgery under local anaesthetic with an oral sedative, describing marginal reflex distance, mild swelling, and a result in which the lids no longer covered the corneal light reflex; a reply described a large improvement.[13]

A Grokipedia account (AI-generated, to be read cautiously) says that in Japan insurance coverage applies where drooping impairs function and does not extend to cosmetic cases, with self-pay clinics doing aesthetic ptosis work at higher cost.[11]

Studies include case series and algorithms for Muller's muscle-conjunctival resection,[3][4] a paediatric 10-year review,[9] and a study correlating vision-related functional impairment with the impact of surgery.[10] Registered trials include a completed 180-participant study of a modified levator tucking technique (NCT04883853),[14] and trials comparing approaches for involutional (NCT03373812)[15] and severe (NCT03916107)[16] ptosis.

Registered trials also include a completed 15-participant trial on managing severe congenital blepharoptosis.[28] The figure that about half of surgical patients needed further surgery within 8-10 years comes from a study summarised by Wikipedia.[12]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, ptosis repair is discussed as a way to open the eye, with first-person surgical accounts.[13]

claims.claim: Ptosis repair gives a more open, more attractive eye.
claims.believers: A poster says the operation uncovered the light reflex that his lids had covered, and a replying member called it a 'big improvement'.[13]
claims.experts: Medical literature frames the operation as functional, and one study correlated vision-related impairment with surgical impact; no study of attractiveness outcomes was found.[10]

claims.claim: Ptosis surgery fixes eye asymmetry and gives a more open eye.
claims.believers: A poster describes lids that had covered the light reflex and no longer did after the operation.[13]
claims.experts: Reviews describe correction of ptosis and eyelid-crease asymmetry as improving cosmetic deformity and lid height, with precise outcomes depending on anatomy and technique.[19]

claims.claim: One operation is a permanent fix.
claims.believers: Forum accounts are mostly of a single repair with a quick recovery.[13]
claims.experts: A study cited by Wikipedia reports that about half of surgical patients needed further surgery within 8-10 years.[12]

claims.believers: A poster reports about half an hour of surgery, brief stinging on injection and swelling the next day.[13]
claims.experts: Trials examine post-operative inflammation and bleeding after eyelid surgery, and risks listed include uneven lids, dry eye, bleeding, infection and rare loss of lid movement.[12][21][22]

claims.claim: Drops can raise a droopy lid without surgery.
claims.believers: Drops are presented as a temporary non-surgical alternative for mild to moderate acquired ptosis.[11]
claims.experts: The FDA approved 0.1% oxymetazoline drops for acquired ptosis in 2020, with a mechanism involving Muller's muscle.[12][30]

chain: Levator tendon is tightened or reattached, or Muller muscle is shortened
More open, less tired-looking eye with more symmetrical lids
angle.text: Ptosis repair raises the lid margin so more of the iris and pupil shows and the lids match each other more closely. People who have it for looks describe a more awake, open eye; the same operation also widens the upper visual field when the drooping lid obstructed vision.
